concepts.name: The Rock Cycle: Concept, Directionality, and Misconceptions
key_dimensions: Whether the rock cycle is unidirectional or cyclical — UPSC trap on 'fixed sequence' assumption
Role of internal (endogenic) vs external (exogenic) forces in driving the cycle
Time scales involved and why the cycle is considered 'open' and dynamic
Comparison with water cycle and carbon cycle in terms of geological significance

concepts.name: Igneous Rock Formation: Intrusive vs Extrusive Classification
key_dimensions: Difference in cooling rates and resultant crystal size — coarse-grained (plutonic) vs fine-grained (volcanic)
Specific landforms: batholiths, laccoliths, sills, dykes (intrusive) vs lava plateaus, volcanic cones (extrusive)
Examples: Granite (intrusive) vs Basalt (extrusive) — frequently confused in UPSC options
Why Deccan Traps are extrusive igneous and not intrusive — common trap question

concepts.name: Types of Igneous Rocks Based on Silica Content: Acidic vs Basic
key_dimensions: Acidic igneous rocks (>65% SiO₂): Granite, Rhyolite — light-colored, less dense, continental crust association
Basic igneous rocks (<52% SiO₂): Basalt, Gabbro — dark-colored, denser, oceanic crust association
Intermediate types: Andesite, Diorite — often ignored but appear in options
UPSC trap: Granite forms continents while Basalt forms ocean floors — isostasy connection

concepts.name: Sedimentary Rock Formation: Processes of Lithification and Diagenesis
key_dimensions: Steps: Weathering → Erosion → Transportation → Deposition → Compaction → Cementation (Lithification)
Diagenesis vs Metamorphism — where one ends and other begins (pressure/temperature threshold)
Difference between clastic, chemical, and biogenic/organic sedimentary rocks with examples
Why sedimentary rocks are called 'secondary rocks' and their fossil-bearing significance

concepts.name: Classification of Sedimentary Rocks: Mechanically Formed, Chemically Formed, and Organically Formed
key_dimensions: Mechanically formed: Sandstone, Conglomerate, Shale — formed by physical deposition of fragments
Chemically formed: Limestone (travertine), Rock salt, Gypsum — precipitation from solution
Organically/Biogenically formed: Coal, Petroleum source rocks, Chalk, Coral limestone
UPSC trap: Limestone can be both chemically AND organically formed — not mutually exclusive

concepts.name: Metamorphic Rock Formation: Agents and Types of Metamorphism
key_dimensions: Three agents: Heat, Pressure, and Chemically active fluids — all three must be contextually understood
Contact (thermal) metamorphism vs Regional (dynamic) metamorphism — scale and depth differences
Cataclastic metamorphism near fault zones — least discussed but appears in options
UPSC trap: Metamorphism does not involve melting — if melting occurs, it becomes magma (migmatite boundary)

concepts.name: Parent Rock to Metamorphic Rock Transformations: Specific Pairs
key_dimensions: Limestone → Marble; Sandstone → Quartzite; Shale → Slate → Phyllite → Schist → Gneiss (progressive metamorphism)
Granite → Gneiss — igneous to metamorphic transformation (commonly asked)
Coal → Graphite — organic sedimentary to metamorphic (carbon structure change)
UPSC trap: Gneiss can form from both sedimentary (shale) AND igneous (granite) parents — not unique to one

concepts.name: Foliation and Non-Foliation in Metamorphic Rocks
key_dimensions: Foliated rocks: Slate, Phyllite, Schist, Gneiss — parallel alignment of minerals due to directed pressure
Non-foliated rocks: Marble, Quartzite, Hornfels — formed under uniform pressure (contact metamorphism)
Why foliation is an indicator of regional metamorphism and tectonic activity
UPSC trap: Marble is non-foliated despite being metamorphic — students confuse all metamorphic rocks as foliated

concepts.name: Role of Magma and Lava in the Rock Cycle: Composition and Behavior
key_dimensions: Magma vs Lava distinction — magma is subsurface molten rock; lava is magma that has reached surface
Magma composition determines volcanic explosivity: silica-rich = viscous = explosive (Rhyolitic); silica-poor = fluid = effusive (Basaltic)
Magmatic differentiation and how one magma body can produce multiple rock types
Connection to plate tectonics: subduction zones produce andesitic magma; mid-ocean ridges produce basaltic magma

concepts.name: Weathering as the Starting Point of the Rock Cycle: Mechanical vs Chemical
key_dimensions: Mechanical weathering: frost action, thermal expansion, exfoliation — dominant in arid/polar climates
Chemical weathering: hydrolysis, oxidation, carbonation, solution — dominant in humid tropical climates
Biological weathering as a bridge between the two — often omitted in standard answers
UPSC trap: Weathering produces regolith, not soil — soil requires additional biological processes (pedogenesis)

concepts.name: Plate Tectonics and the Rock Cycle: Interconnections
key_dimensions: Subduction zones: oceanic crust melts → magma → igneous rocks (drives igneous part of cycle)
Collision zones: high pressure-temperature → metamorphic rocks (Himalayas = metamorphic terrain)
Rifting/divergent boundaries: new basaltic crust formation — seafloor spreading connection
UPSC trap: The rock cycle operates WITHOUT plate tectonics on smaller scales too (surface processes) — not exclusively plate-driven

concepts.name: Economic Significance of Rock Types and Their Cycle-Stage Association
key_dimensions: Sedimentary rocks: host 90% of fossil fuels (coal, petroleum, natural gas) — economic geology significance
Metamorphic rocks: host metallic minerals — gold in greenstone belts, graphite, mica (Jharkhand, Rajasthan)
Igneous rocks: host minerals like chromite, magnetite, platinum group elements in mafic/ultramafic rocks
UPSC trap: Diamond occurs in Kimberlite — an igneous rock, NOT a metamorphic rock despite extreme pressure formation

concepts.name: Sedimentary Structures as Indicators of Past Environments
key_dimensions: Stratification/bedding planes as indicators of depositional environment and time
Cross-bedding indicates ancient river/wind deposition; graded bedding indicates turbidity currents
Fossils in sedimentary rocks as tools for relative dating (biostratigraphy)
UPSC relevance: Gondwana coal fields of India — sedimentary origin, Permian-Carboniferous age, peninsular India

concepts.name: Indian Rock Types and Their Geological Significance: Regional Examples
key_dimensions: Peninsular India: Archean crystalline basement — gneisses, schists, granites (oldest rocks in India)
Deccan Traps: Cretaceous-Paleocene basaltic lava flows — extrusive igneous, covers ~500,000 sq km
Gondwana formations: Sedimentary — contains 98% of India's coal reserves (Damodar, Mahanadi valleys)
UPSC trap: Aravallis are among the oldest fold mountains with metamorphic and igneous rocks — not sedimentary like Himalayas

concepts.name: Rock Cycle and Soil Formation: Pedogenesis Connection
key_dimensions: Parent rock (regolith) → Residual soil vs Transported soil distinction
Basaltic parent rock → Black cotton soil (Regur) in Deccan; Granite/Gneiss → Red laterite soils
Role of climate, organisms, topography, time alongside parent rock (Jenny's CLORPT factors)
UPSC trap: Laterite soil forms from leaching of silica — it is a product of chemical weathering, NOT a sedimentary rock itself

concepts.name: Carbon Cycle and Rock Cycle Intersection: Geological Carbon Storage
key_dimensions: Carbonate rocks (limestone, dolomite) as long-term carbon sinks — geological carbon sequestration
Weathering of silicate rocks consumes CO₂ (carbon-silicate cycle) — climate regulation over geological time
Volcanism releases CO₂ back into atmosphere — geological carbon source
UPSC relevance: Carbon capture in rocks vs biological carbon sinks — comparison in climate change context

concepts.name: Unconformities in Rock Record: Types and Significance
key_dimensions: Angular unconformity, disconformity, nonconformity — represent gaps in geological record
Unconformities indicate periods of erosion, uplift, or non-deposition between rock cycle phases
Great Unconformity — global significance as evidence of major erosion event
UPSC relevance: Unconformities in Vindhyan Supergroup and their significance in Indian stratigraphy

concepts.name: Metamorphic Grade and Index Minerals: Progressive Metamorphism
key_dimensions: Barrovian zones: Chlorite → Biotite → Garnet → Staurolite → Kyanite → Sillimanite (increasing grade)
Index minerals as proxies for temperature-pressure conditions — geothermobarometry concept
Low-grade vs high-grade metamorphism and resultant rock types (Slate vs Gneiss)
UPSC trap: High-grade metamorphism approaching melting point produces Migmatite — a hybrid rock, neither purely metamorphic nor igneous

concepts.name: Rock Cycle and Geomorphological Landforms: Process-Form Relationships
key_dimensions: Differential weathering of rock types creates landforms: Inselbergs in granite, Karst in limestone, Mesas in sandstone
Hard igneous/metamorphic rocks → Resistant ridges; Soft sedimentary rocks → Valleys (ridge-and-valley topography)
Joints and bedding planes in rocks control drainage patterns — rectangular (joints) vs trellis (sedimentary dip)
UPSC trap: Bornhardts/Inselbergs form in granite — an igneous rock, through exfoliation (onion weathering), not in sedimentary terrain

concepts.name: Isostasy and Rock Density Differences: Crustal Equilibrium
key_dimensions: Granitic (sialic) continental crust — less dense (2.7 g/cm³) vs Basaltic (simatic) oceanic crust — denser (3.0 g/cm³)
Isostatic adjustment after erosion (unloading) — uplift of continental regions over geological time
Why continents 'float' higher than ocean floors despite being older — density-based buoyancy in mantle
UPSC trap: Isostasy is NOT the same as plate tectonics — isostasy is vertical adjustment; tectonics involves lateral movement
